Review: By the time they released "Amplified Heart" in 1994, Ben Watt and Tracey Thorn had spent a decade churning out admired but relatively commercially unsuccessful "lite-jazz" albums. Then, on the back of a string of on-point club remixes (Todd Terry's chart-topping version of "Missing" included), the set surprisingly became a runaway success. To celebrate the album's 25th birthday, "Amplified Heart" has been given the audiophile reissue treatment. It suits the album's gently breezy, emotion-rich feel, with Thorn's evocative, lovelorn vocals perfectly matching Watt's sunset-friendly blend of acoustic guitars, soft-touch double bass, trip-hop style beats and Balearic-minded electronics. It remains one of the duo's greatest albums and should be in every discerning listener's collection.

Review: This album is more than a greatest hits, it's a story of how two artists kept evolving while never losing their core. Spanning over four decades, the 16-song set opens with the kinetic energy of their club-era triumphs, most notably the Todd Terry remix of 'Missing' and works its way back through trip-hop shadings, d&b experiments and, eventually, the intimate, jazz-inflected beginnings. The fast side is all pulse and polish, with their flair for dance-floor melancholia, while the slow side lets Tracey Thorn's unmistakable voice take center stage in more vulnerable, stripped-down settings. Between Watt's inventive production and Thorn's rich, emotionally unguarded delivery is the hook of the duo. Whether in the sharp synth edges of Fuse's 'Run a Red Light' or the smoky intimacy of 'Night and Day'. The Best of Everything But the Girl shows how the pair's talent and adaptability have kept them vital for more than 40 years.

Review: Formed in 1982 in Hull, East Yorkshire, Tracey Thorn's and Ben Watt's star as Everything But The Girl is burning brightly to this day. Perhaps the key to their survival has been to be ill afraid to embrace change and push themselves creatively. This 16-song record spans their 40-year-plus career, from their indie jazz-folk debut Night and Day to 2023's forward-thinking electronica record Fuse. The sequencing is purposefully paced so that they start with fast bangers and wind down with the ballads. They come out of the traps with the era-defining 1994 hit 'Missing (Todd Terry remix)' - "And I miss you, like the deserts miss the rain" - and culminate with the jangly bedsit pop of title track 'Night and Day'. To hear how they got to where they've got to only serves to heighten how precious their back catalogue is.
